metadata.title: An axiomatic basis for computer programming
metadata.abstract_summary: A program's correctness can be proven from axioms and inference rules applied to precondition/postcondition assertions about its statements (Hoare logic), giving programming a deductive, mathematical foundation - the origin of formal program verification as a discipline.

sections.heading: Claims
sections.text:
As the authors state it:

> In this paper an attempt is made to explore the logical foundations of computer programming by use of techniques which were first applied in the study of geometry and have later been extended to other branches of mathematics. This involves the elucidation of sets of axioms and rules of inference which can be used in proofs of the properties of computer programs. Examples are given of such axioms and rules, and a formal proof of a simple theorem is displayed. Finally, it is argued that important advantage, both theoretical and practical, may follow from a pursuance of these topics.

sections.heading: Method
sections.text: Presents an axiom for assignment and inference rules for sequential composition, iteration (introducing the loop invariant), and conditionals; argues soundness informally and demonstrates the method with a full correctness proof of a real algorithm (Russian peasant multiplication).

sections.heading: Evidence & Limits
sections.text:
- A foundational logic paper, not an empirical one - its "evidence" is the internal soundness of the proof system, not an experiment.
- The paper itself flags open problems (a fully rigorous treatment of side effects, procedure calls, jumps) that took the field another decade-plus to resolve.
- The practical scalability of Hoare-style proofs to large real programs was, and remains, a genuinely hard, only partially automated problem - the paper establishes the method, not that it scales for free.
